concept: Grain is what one row represents. Joining two one-to-many tables can multiply rows and inflate sums unless you align the grain first.
example:
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Amount) AS Revenue
    FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID
), TicketTotals AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS TicketCount
    FROM Tickets GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT c.CustomerID, COALESCE(o.Revenue, 0) AS Revenue,
       COALESCE(t.TicketCount, 0) AS TicketCount
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN OrderTotals o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
LEFT JOIN TicketTotals t ON c.CustomerID = t.CustomerID;
breakdown: Orders has one row per order; Tickets has one row per ticket.
Joining both raw tables on CustomerID multiplies matching order and ticket combinations.
Each CTE reduces a source to one row per customer.
The final joins preserve customer grain and avoid double counting.
practice: Explain why a customer with 2 orders and 3 tickets could show 6 joined rows. Then write a query that counts orders and tickets separately.
answer:
WITH O AS (SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID),
T AS (SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS TicketCount FROM Tickets GROUP BY CustomerID)
SELECT c.CustomerID, COALESCE(O.OrderCount, 0) AS OrderCount,
       COALESCE(T.TicketCount, 0) AS TicketCount
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN O ON c.CustomerID = O.CustomerID
LEFT JOIN T ON c.CustomerID = T.CustomerID;
takeaways: Always state output grain before writing joins.
Pre-aggregate separate fact tables to a common grain.

check.question: Why can joining order headers to order lines inflate a header-level revenue total?
options: Each header may be repeated once for every matching line.
LEFT JOIN automatically removes duplicate headers.
A join changes numeric values stored in the source table.
GROUP BY always preserves original row counts.

deep_dive.heading: Diagnosing one-to-many join inflation
paragraphs: Before joining, state the intended output grain in one sentence: one row per customer, case, invoice, or line item. A join between cases and case items produces multiple rows per case, which can inflate case-level amounts.
Diagnose multiplicity with COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT key) before and after each join. Aggregate child tables to the intended grain before joining when you need case-level measures.
DISTINCT is not a general repair: it may hide legitimate duplicate-looking transactions and cannot undo a duplicated SUM.
questions: How would you detect cases with no items?
What is the expected row count after the join if Cases has one row per CaseID?
deep_dive.code:
WITH ItemTotals AS (
    SELECT CaseID, SUM(LineAmount) AS ItemRevenue
    FROM CaseItems
    GROUP BY CaseID
)
SELECT c.CaseID, c.CustomerID, i.ItemRevenue
FROM Cases AS c
LEFT JOIN ItemTotals AS i ON i.CaseID = c.CaseID;
